questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Pretty easy through the WOKO dorm. You just sign up for the opportunity and will get an email with an offer if there is any available which there usually is.
You can also sign up for an “apartment swap”, where you swap with a Swiss student who is going to Denmark.
Otherwise, there are local sites where you can search for apartments just like in Denmark (google)
WOKO also has this service, where you can also find people who are going on exchange stays and rent their room for a semester:
https://www.woko.ch/en/untermieter-gesucht
ETH has a pretty good guide on their website regarding housing search.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I lived in a WOKO dormitory, which I was super super happy about, but there are both good and bad sides to it, which is up to you to judge for yourself:

This is related to the social aspect, but 99% of my friends here in Switzerland come from the dormitory. The rooms are only for exchange students, so everyone starts at the same time and everyone is new together. It is easy to make friends, and it is super nice to have someone who is in the same boat as you, and where you can go down together for residence permits, the office, etc. If you are bored or feel lonely, there is almost always someone in the kitchen you can go down to and talk to. Every weekend there is someone who goes on a trip somewhere that you can join. The rooms are super nice, and I have my own sink, which is a huge lifesaver. The kitchen and toilets are professionally cleaned every morning. 

The bad: we were 160ish students sharing a kitchen so it is pretty much always extremely dirty despite the daily kitchen cleaning twice a day. It is not for the faint of heart and I always wash pots/pans/equipment before using it. The fridges are extremely small (you get a small locked box) so you have to cook almost every day as you can't really have leftovers and there is no freezer.

We share a bathroom in each hallway (around 20ish per bathroom with 3 toilet stalls). Some people are not hygienic and you can see some unfortunate things…. 

Our dormitory at Altstetten (20 min away from Zentrum) has also been subjected to harassment and some have even experienced violence directed at them by a local gang of men (this was reported to the police multiple times, but they were very very slow to take action). After the dorm hired private security guards there have not been cases since, but you should be aware that large student buildings can be a target for local aggressive groups of teenagers and young men who know that international students are easier victims. Personally, I've never experienced anything, but it's still something to keep in mind if you're going home late. In general, Zurich is as safe as Copenhagen, but there are some rougher areas, including where my dorm is, which might be worth checking out if you're the type of person who's out late often.

WOKO are also quite dishonest about their deposit practices so remember to take pictures of every inch of the room when you arrive. I know multiple people who got big deductions in their deposit from stuff that was already damaged in the room despite already having documented those damages in the beginning (and deductions such as from a dusty shelf). They had to further dispute those deductions. Some people also got their deducted for things that were objectively not damaged in the room, so also remember to take pictures of every object and surface before you leave. I also got deducted from things already present in the room, but unfortunately I did not take pictures of that in the beginning as I initially thought it was super small stuff that didn't matter. 

What you decide to do depends a lot on who you are as a person. I personally do not regret taking up a student dorm just because of all the friends I made here.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: This is very specific for pharmaceutical sciences, but since I decided to take block courses that were not electives (but mandatory courses for the master's students at ETH), I had to email the department coordinator for permission to enroll which was quite confusing. We got an email that we had to enroll by checking the box outside the course, but the courses I planned did not have that option so I had to email a few different people to get enrolled.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The exchange coordinators were super helpful and quick to answer. In general all the administrative staff at ETH were quick and efficient so I recommend emailing them if you need any help or have questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses that I wanted

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take advantage of the fact that only 2/3rd of the courses have to be within your faculty. I took all of my courses within pharmaceutical sciences because that is what I found the least confusing but I wish I had spent more time researching what courses were available - for example there is a course programme called "Science in perspective" in which they (in my semester) studied gothic literature. There really is a very wide variety of courses available at ETH and it is a good opportunity to try something new that you might not do at home.

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
To be honest, most if not all the courses in pharmaceutical sciences were academically below what you would find at KU. We had 10 courses in 1 block / half a semester, which meant that every course was super small and superficial. I did not learn a lot of new material. 
The research project that I later did (at master's level) was equivalent to or even below a bachelor level project at KU.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Style of teaching was pretty similar - mostly a mixture of lectures, group work, and case work / discussions in class. Maybe a bit more lecture oriented than UCPH though it depends on your courses and home degree.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I do not recommend any courses that I took except my course in biostatistics.
You learn a lot about how to use the programme R to solve problems in real scientific research which I found very insightful and useful. But it is a block course so it might be hard to fit into the schedule of someone taking semester courses - it was a total of 3 days of teaching times 9 hours. For the exam, you had to analyse and answer some question retaining to a real research paper which was super interesting since the material felt very applicable to real research.
If you're doing a research project over here, then I recommend that you go to the ETH website and look at the projects and professors etc. on the website itself. You are told that you can use the website:
https://sirop.org/app/
, (which you can!), but it doesn't show everything there is. I only used this page myself, and only later found out that many research groups do not use that website at all, so your best option is to simply write an email to the professors you think are working on something interesting and ask.
You should also be aware that a full working week is 43-45 hours in Switzerland and not the 37 you know from Denmark. I ended up working 9-10 hours a day in my research group which is unfortunately not uncommon (even though they bragged about how "flexible" my schedule would be).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Public transport is very very expensive, way more than I first expected. You can get the local monthly pass to go to school and travel in the central part of Zürich for about 500-600 DKK which is pretty affordable BUT if you ever decide to go outside Zürich it will cost a lot.  For example, without any deals/add-ons etc., going to a nearby city Luzern (40 min by train), costs 30CHF x 2 for a single trip, which is about 500 DKK. I travelled basically every weekend and as much as possible, so I spend a lot on public transport. There are some ways to make it cheaper though:
Get the half fare card as soon as you're able. It is a card in which you pay for upfront, and then you get 50% of every subsequent ticket and special day ticket deals. The pricing is different if you're under 25. If you turn 25 before going to Switzerland, I recommend buying the half-fare card beforehand online because it lasts for a year from when you buy it and is valid even after you turn 25. 
You can also get the night GA for 99CHF if you're under  25 years, which enables free travel all over the country after 19.00 or before 05.00. 
If you're under 25 years old, you can also get the Friend's Ticket which enables 4 friends under 25 yo, to buy a day ticket for 4, for 80CHF, which means you can travel the entire country for only 20CHF a day. The cheapest way to travel. So you can go from Zurich to Geneva for 20CHF per person round trip when a normal round trip ticket costs 200CHF. Even if you can’t find exactly 3 other people, it can often be worth it, even if you’re only 2 or 3 friends. Here it is an advantage to live in a dormitory, as there’s always someone who’s keen to go on a trip with you, so you can split the price.
It is quite expensive to be above 25 years old when going to Switzerland. 

Eating at restaurants is quite expensive in Zürich (not unusual to pay 30CHF-40CHF for a meal in an average restaurant) and the food is often not that good anyways. 

Going to the doctor can also easily be 200CHF to 300CHF. If you're a member of the EU, you get it refunded (except for a payment of 92CHF), but you still have to pay the price upfront.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Some fruits/berries and vegetables are actually cheaper than in Denmark. If you're able to shop at a Lidl or Aldi you will be able to find prices comparable to Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Students of ETH and UZH have the sports organisation of ASVZ which enables you to join 100+ sports for free and the gym for free. It is very popular though, and you have to sign up early. Popular sports classes like spinning have a 50/50 chance of entering because you sign up through a lottery system. Though outside that ETH has surprisingly few groups that I found interesting - a lot of them were language groups, buisness/entrepeneur/start up related. Not really any creative or a lot of hobby related opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really recommend hiking since the swiss nature is just so beautiful. There are hiking routes for all levels and you do not need previous experience. ETH has some hiking groups though I did not attend any, and I just went with my friends from the dorm. 

I also recommend getting a KulturLegi for Zürich. It is a card that allows you to get into a lot of cultural events heavily discounted (like the cinema, museums etc). You just have to apply online and attach proof that you have recieved a scholarship from the state (the SEMP scholarship paper)

ESN Zürich hosts A LOT of events which I heavily recommend. With ESN you get to go on trips you would not otherwise have gone on for super cheap. It is also a great opportunity to make new friends. Just sign up on the website and watch out for which events are running since there is often limited seats.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking and visiting all the beautiful Swiss towns.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy as I think Swiss culture is very similar to Northern European culture. The swiss are a bit closed off and it can be hard to make local friends, which is why

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Attend local events such as painting class. I was able to meet a few local people that way.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really any.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: How clean and punctual everyone is. The nature is spotless and everything administrative or customer service related is extremely efficient, way more than in Denmark!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Apply for a lot of grant money before going, get into the Swiss nature, be open to make a lot of new friends in the beginning (so you can also travel for cheap).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take the German Intensive language course in the beginning. It is really nice to start out with a class of other exchange and foreign students that you are together with every day. The language course also makes you go out into the city and gives you information about basic stuff such as the culture and local history of the city.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many new people and being able to experience the amazing nature in Switzerland. I was not an outdoor type person before.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Adminstrative stuff associated with the exchange.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
